import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

An app whose people work together (a chat, a docs editor, a CRM, a game
lobby) keeps three kinds of things, and each one has its place. Putting one
in the wrong place is the most common mistake, and on Calimero Cloud it shows
up as:

```text
403 FORBIDDEN: a session opened on an app's frontend can use that app only; do this on the cluster's own page
```

This page says where each thing goes, what your frontend may change on its
own, what it must send to the node's consent page, and why. The rules
themselves, route by route, are in
[Sessions & authority](/protocol/sessions-and-authority/).

## The three places

```text
Organization "Acme"                     ③ the organization's: everyone's, every app's
├── members, org roles (owner/admin/member/guest), org-wide capabilities
├── invites, name, deletion
│
├── Chat's app team                     ② your app's own teams: your frontend runs them
│   ├── #general   open team    ── instance of chat (access: team #general)
│   ├── #design    open team    ── instance of chat
│   └── #secret    closed team  ── instance of chat
│
└── Docs' app team                      another app's teams: not yours
    └── …

inside each instance                    ① your app's state: your code runs it
    messages, reactions, pins, a moderator list, per-account settings
```

| | ① App state | ② The app's own teams | ③ The organization |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | Rows in one instance, written by your app's methods | Your package's [app team](/protocol/organizations/#app-teams) in the org, and the teams you make below it | The org itself: who is in it, their org role and org-wide capabilities, invites |
| Who enforces it | Your code (`env::caller()`, guards), inside the instance | The node, before your code runs: someone outside a team never reaches an instance whose access is that team | The node, for every app in the org |
| Your frontend changes it | Yes, by calling your methods | Yes, directly (`orgs.teamCreate`, `teamSetMember`, ...) | No: it asks the node's consent page |
| Use it for | Content, and rules that only your app understands | Rooms, channels, folders, boards, DMs: anything with its own member list that must be **private** from others in the org; your app's admins and permissions | Making the workspace, inviting, joining, org admins, removing someone from the org, renaming or deleting it |

The rule of thumb:

- **Private between people in the same org?** Then it is a team, below your app team, with its own instance.
- **Only means something to your app?** Then it is your app team's (a team row: lead, capabilities) or your app's state, never the organization's.
- **Affects other apps or the org as a whole?** Then it is the organization's, and your frontend asks for it on the consent page.

## Why it is not all inside the app

It would be simpler if an app could manage everything about its users itself.
Three things stop that, and each one is a guarantee the people using your app
rely on.

**1. The organization is shared by every app in it.** Acme's people, their
roles and their invites are the same in Chat, Docs and the CRM, and in
Calimero Home, which is where the org is administered. "Admin" in the org
means admin of every app in it. If Chat could make someone an org admin, or
remove someone from the org, it would be changing Docs and the CRM too.
So an app changes only what is its own (②), and org-wide changes are made
where everyone can see what they are agreeing to (③).

**2. A passkey prompt is blind.** The authenticator shows the site's name and
"Use your passkey?", never what the request commits to. Whichever page runs
the ceremony decides what the person believes they are approving. An app's
frontend is its publisher's code. If it could run the step-up for an
org-wide change, a buggy or malicious page could show "Create channel" and
have the passkey sign "Make Mallory an owner". So org-wide changes are
approved on the **node's** [consent page](/protocol/consent-page/): served
from the node's own origin, compiled into `merod`, showing what was frozen
from node state, never what the app said. The app can ask; it cannot word
the question.

**3. Privacy inside one instance is only as good as the app's code.** An
instance's data is one replicated state. The node decides who reaches the
instance at all (its access: `org`, a team, a list of accounts); inside it,
only your methods decide who reads what. A private channel kept as a flag in
a shared instance is private only while every method, view and event of the
app gets it right. A private channel that is its own instance, reached
through a closed team, is private because the node never lets anyone else in.

That is why the split exists: your frontend has a free hand over your app's
state and your app's own teams, because nothing there can reach beyond your
app; everything that can, goes to the person on a page your app does not
control.

## What your frontend may change on its own

A person who signs in on your package's frontend origin (served by the node,
or [registered](/protocol/identities/#registered-origins)) holds a session
**bound to your package** (`me().app` is your package's name). A session
opened on the cluster's own page, `meroctl`, or a dev node without
`--apps-domain` is **unbound** and may call every route; see
[Test as your users will](#test-as-your-users-will).

A bound session may, with the person's own authority:

| Do | Call |
| --- | --- |
| Call and read your package's instances; create new ones | your methods; `apps.create({ package, org, access })` |
| Make a room below your app team | `orgs.teamCreate({ org, parent: appTeam, name, join: 'everyone' \| 'invite' })` |
| Rename it, open or close it, move it (within your teams) | `orgs.teamUpdate({ org, team, name?, join?, parent? })` |
| Add or remove someone, make them lead, give them capabilities there, on your app team or a team below it | `orgs.teamSetMember({ org, team, account, lead?, role?, capabilities? })`, `orgs.teamRemoveMember({ org, team, account })` (passkey) |
| Delete a room, with its instances | `orgs.teamDelete({ org, team })` (passkey when apps go with it) |
| Move one of your instances from one of your teams to another | `apps.access({ app, access: { kind: 'team', team } })` |
| Set the person's display name in the org | `orgs.memberMetadata({ org, account, metadata })` |
| Ask for anything else | `client.openConsentPage(...)` |

Whether the person *may* is still judged by the log: a member who is not a
lead of `#secret` cannot add people to it from any page.

## What goes through the consent page

| The person wants to | Consent kind (mero-js builder) |
| --- | --- |
| Create a workspace (comes with your app team) | `createOrg` (`createOrgConsent`) |
| Invite someone / join with an invite | `createInvite`, `acceptInvite` |
| Make someone an org admin, or change their org role | `setMemberRole` |
| Remove someone from the whole org / leave it | `removeMember` / `leaveOrg` |
| Rename or delete the org | `renameOrg` / `deleteOrg` |
| Change org-wide capabilities or a member's org-wide capabilities | `setCapabilities` |
| Put someone in several teams at once | `setMemberTeams`, `removeMemberTeams` |
| Revoke an invite | `revokeInvite` |
| Upgrade the app, approve a release or outbound hosts | `upgrade`, `release`, `outbound` |

The page is a full-page redirect: keep what you were doing in
`sessionStorage`, call `openConsentPage`, and when the node sends the person
back, read the decision with `resumeConsent()`, never from the URL. See
[Ask for consent](/build/guides/frontends/#ask-for-consent).

Some things have no consent kind and are not for an app's frontend at all:
deleting, transferring or moving an instance, changing an instance's access
other than between your own teams, giving packages app teams in an existing
org, API keys, passkeys. Those belong to the person's own tools: Calimero
Home, the cluster's page, or `meroctl`.

## Recipes

**Channels, rooms, folders, boards.** One closed or open team below your app
team per room, and one instance per room with `access: { kind: 'team', team }`.
The person who makes the team leads it, so they can create its instance and
add people.

```ts
const appTeam = consentOutcome.teamId; // from createOrg, or GET /orgs/{org}/app-teams
const { teamId } = await client.orgs.teamCreate({ org, parent: appTeam, name: 'secret', join: 'invite' });
const { appId } = await client.apps.create({ package: 'chat', org, access: { kind: 'team', team: teamId } });
await client.orgs.teamSetMember({ org, team: teamId, account: bob }, { confirm: passkeyConfirm(passkey) });
```

Removing someone from your app team takes their rows in every team below it,
so "remove from Chat" also removes them from its private channels.

**Your app's admins and permissions.** Make them **leads** of your app team, or
give them capabilities on their app-team row (`teamSetMember({ lead: true })`,
`teamSetMember({ capabilities })`). `CREATE_CHILD_TEAM` on the app team is
"may create channels". `teamSetMember` writes the whole row: send `lead`,
`role` and `capabilities` together, as a missing `lead` is `false`. Keep finer roles that only your app understands (a
channel moderator, who may pin) in your app's state, checked in your methods.

**A DM.** A closed team of two below the app team, and its instance.

**One shared instance.** If nothing in it is private between members (a
whiteboard, a game table everyone at the table sees), keep one instance on
your app team and use app state. Make it a team the moment some of it must be
hidden from some members.

## Mistakes to avoid

These are all in apps today, and all fail from a bound session.

| Instead of | Do |
| --- | --- |
| `orgs.capabilities({ org, account, capabilities })` for an app permission ("may create channels") | `orgs.teamSetMember({ org, team: appTeam, account, capabilities })` |
| `orgs.setMember({ role: 'admin' })` to make an app admin | `orgs.teamSetMember({ org, team: appTeam, account, lead: true })`; org admin only through `setMemberRole` |
| A private room as an instance with `access: { kind: 'accounts', accounts }`, members changed with `apps.access` | a closed team below the app team; members with `teamSetMember` |
| `apps.delete` to delete a room | `orgs.teamDelete` of its team |
| `orgs.teamCreate` without `parent` | `parent` = your app team or a team below it |
| `orgs.create`, `orgs.inviteCreate`, `orgs.inviteRedeem` | `createOrg`, `createInvite`, `acceptInvite` on the consent page |
| `orgs.removeMember` to remove someone from the app | `orgs.teamRemoveMember` on your app team (from the whole org: `removeMember` on the consent page) |
| `orgs.metadata` for the workspace name | the org's name at `createOrg`; `renameOrg` to change it |

## Limitations

- **Your app needs its app team in the org.** A workspace made with
  `createOrg` from your frontend comes with it (clusters on 1.0.0-rc.22 or
  later). An org made elsewhere, or before, has none until an admin adds it
  from an unbound session (`POST /orgs/{org}/app-teams`, Calimero Home);
  until then your frontend cannot create teams there.
- **A team's default capabilities** (`orgs.capabilities({ team })`) cannot be
  set from a bound session, even on your own app team, and there is no
  consent kind for it yet. Set capabilities on each row instead.
- **Your app team itself** (its name, openness, mark) is the org admins', not
  your frontend's. You manage the teams below it and the rows in it.
- **Instances**: a bound session cannot delete, transfer or move an instance,
  or change its access except between your own teams. Delete through the
  room's team.
- **Existing private rooms made with an account list** cannot be turned into
  teams from your frontend; do it once from an unbound session.
- **The consent page** is a redirect, lives 10 minutes, and an account has one
  undecided request per node (a new one replaces it). Batch what you ask for.

## Test as your users will

On a dev node without `--apps-domain`, or signed in on the node's own origin,
your session is **unbound** and every call above succeeds: you will not see
these 403s until Cloud. Test bound:

1. Run the node with an apps domain (`merod local` serves frontends at
   `{label}.localhost`).
2. Open your frontend on its served origin and sign in there.
3. Check `(await client.auth.me()).app` is your package's name.
4. Run your end-to-end flows: create a workspace, make a private room, add and
   remove a member, delete the room, leave.

Your frontend can tell which kind it holds (`me().app` set or not) and call
the routes directly when unbound, as a dev tool or the cluster's own page may
do, and go through the consent page when bound.
